extraction.name: ChartQA
extraction.description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 machine-generated questions over 20,882 real-world charts curated from four online sources.
extraction.creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
extraction.citeAs: Masry, Ahmed; Long, Do Xuan; Tan, Jia Qing; Joty, Shafiq; Hoque, Enamul. ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv:2203.10244v1, 2022.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was constructed by crawling real-world charts from four online sources: Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD. For Pew, only chart images were crawled because underlying data tables were not available. For the other three sources, the authors extracted underlying data tables, metadata such as title and chart type, SVG files, and associated text descriptions. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models. The dataset includes two annotation procedures: collecting human-authored question-answer pairs using Amazon Mechanical Turk and generating question-answer pairs automatically from Statista human-written chart summaries using T5 models, followed by heuristic filtering and manual validation of a subset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of real-world chart images from Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD; for three of these sources the authors also extracted underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and associated text descriptions; for Pew only chart images were available.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors extracted bounding boxes of chart elements from SVG files, adapted ChartOCR to extract fully structured data tables from chart images, used CRAFT to recognize chart text, and associated data values with text labels using positional and color information. For machine-generated QA pairs, they fine-tuned T5 models for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation on SQuAD, generated questions from human-written chart summaries, filtered invalid questions using a heuristic that removed questions whose answers could not be found in the chart data table, manually analyzed 1,250 QA pairs for quality, and manually cleaned the machine-generated test set by removing invalid questions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For source data, the authors extracted underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, associated text descriptions, and bounding boxes of chart elements. For human-authored QA collection, charts were presented so that data labels of chart elements were visible to workers. For machine-generated QA, human-written summaries were used as input to T5-based answer extraction and question generation models, then invalid questions were filtered out if the answer could not be found in the chart data table. Both human-written and machine-generated QA pairs were randomly split into train, validation, and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-authored QA pairs were collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers were asked to focus on two types of questions for each chart image: compositional questions involving at least two mathematical or logical operations, and visual questions referring to visual attributes such as color, height, and length of graphical marks. For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was considered correct; otherwise, the authors manually checked the answers to select the final correct answer. For machine-generated QA, questions were generated from Statista human-written summaries using two T5 models: one for answer extraction and one for answer-aware question generation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For human-authored QA, overall agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. The paper notes that exact match does not account for typos or lexical variations such as '3$' vs. '3 dollars' or '86.33' vs. '86.3'. After manually checking 500 random samples, agreement was found to be 78.55% when typos and lexical variations were considered. For machine-generated QA, after heuristic filtering, the authors manually analyzed 1,250 QA pairs and found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct given the chart. The machine-generated test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 questions per chart from one worker, with each question answered by another annotator
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5000 accomplished HITs; workers were further filtered using a pre-test. The paper also states compensation was based on the U.S. minimum wage.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5, fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The chart sources cover topics including social and economic issues, demographic trends, public opinion, politics, economy, health, and society. The paper states that annotator annotations were anonymized to protect privacy.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that their models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications, and they cannot guarantee that model outputs will always be correct. They also hope the benchmark will help address challenges in visual and logical reasoning over charts.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes topic imbalance across sources, for example politics is common among all sources and nearly half of Pew charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type across datasets. The machine-generated questions may include invalid or unanswerable questions because of mismatch between training and test domains, though filtering and manual cleaning were applied.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark is challenging because human-written questions exhibit informal language, typos, lexical variation, and complex visual and compositional reasoning. Automatic data extraction from real-world charts remains error-prone and performance drops when gold tables are not provided. Pie charts and some line charts are harder due to higher extraction errors. The authors note that current models cannot effectively handle nested operations and that their models may produce incorrect outputs. They also state that they cannot guarantee model outputs will always be correct.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a benchmark for chart question answering, especially for training, validation, and testing models that perform visual and logical reasoning over charts. The paper provides train, validation, and test splits for both human-authored (ChartQA-H) and machine-generated (ChartQA-M) subsets and uses the dataset to evaluate transformer-based QA models.
